At 1.5x those same five fire near their highs: 5/10 instead of 0/10.

_note: Channel listener (telegram_listener.mjs). Reads public signal channels
over MTProto and feeds any Solana mint it sees into the ordinary audit
pipeline.
SECURITY MODEL: channel text is DATA, never instruction. The listener
extracts base58 mints with a regex and discards everything else — it
does not follow links, act on commands, or trust any claim a channel
makes about a token. Every address goes through the same audit, shield
and insider pipeline as a discovered one, so a channel posting a rug
gets the rug verdict, not an alert.
requiresLogin: MTProto needs a USER session, not a bot token — bots
cannot read channels they do not administer. Run 'node
telegram_listener.mjs --login' yourself to produce a session string;
it asks for your phone, an SMS code and your 2FA password. Nobody else
should ever run that for you, and the session string it prints grants
full access to your Telegram account — treat it like a password.
channels: @usernames, t.me links or numeric ids. An empty list means
the listener watches every chat the session can see, which is noisy;
name the channels you actually want.
_maxQueueLengthNote: Raised 40 -> 500 on 2026-08-09 for zero-miss channel coverage. This is the
ONLY queue in the codebase that drops surfaced tokens: AuditQueue.push()
returns false and increments `dropped` once items.length hits this cap.
A `discovery.maxQueueLength` was requested alongside it and deliberately
NOT added: nothing reads that key. Discovery does not queue — it surfaces
~127 candidates per tick, filters them through filters.* and the audit
cooldown, and slices to scanLimit within the same pass. Adding the key
would have produced a setting that reads as protection and does nothing,
which is the failure blacklist.mjs exists to warn about.
WHAT 500 COSTS. The queue drains one mint every minSecondsBetweenScans (4),
so the cap is also a latency bound: 40 items is 2.7 minutes to drain, 500
is 33 MINUTES. This does not stop tokens being missed so much as convert
a drop into a delay, and a mint audited 33 minutes after a channel posted
it has no timing edge left — it will usually have been surfaced by
discovery long before the queue reaches it. Lower minSecondsBetweenScans
to drain faster, at proportionally more RPC pressure.
The old cap dropped the NEWEST arrivals and kept the queue's head, which
preserved the earliest sightings — the ones with an edge. That behaviour
is unchanged; there is simply far more room before it engages.
NOT CURRENTLY REACHABLE EITHER WAY: the listener needs MTProto user
credentials and TELEGRAM_API_ID, TELEGRAM_API_HASH and TELEGRAM_SESSION
are all absent from .env, so telegram_listener.mjs cannot start and this
queue never fills. Run 'node telegram_listener.mjs --login' yourself to
produce a session before any channel coverage setting has an effect.

_note: Cadence for loop.mjs. 30s is the TARGET, not the achieved rate: a full
pass measured 40-55s, and discovery is a fixed cost that does not shrink
with scanLimit. The loop skips a tick when the previous scan is still
running, so the real cadence tracks scan duration and skipped ticks are
reported rather than hidden.
To get closer to 30s: lower scanLimit and trim discovery.searchQueries.
RPC BUDGET: this runs ~2000 scans/day vs ~120 on the 12-minute task.
_scanLimitNote: Raised 8 -> 15 on 2026-08-09 for wider coverage. READ WHAT IT DOES AND
DOES NOT DO before expecting more throughput from it.
scanLimit is a CEILING on tokens audited per pass, not a target and not a
concurrency setting — concurrency is auditConcurrency (4). MEASURED over
the last 25 ticks of loop.log, the ceiling was not the binding constraint:
tick 96-120  audited 3-6 tokens per pass against a limit of 8
pass duration 34-77s, typically 47-63s
~127 candidates surfaced per tick (60 launch feeds + ~66 search)
So of ~127 surfaced, only 3-6 survive to be audited, and the limit of 8
was never reached. Raising it to 15 therefore changes nothing on a typical
tick; it only helps on the rare pass where more than 8 candidates clear
everything upstream of it.
WHAT ACTUALLY BOUNDS COVERAGE, in the order the pipeline applies it:
1. filters.*            — minLiquidityUsd, the mcap band, maxAgeHours
and minTxns24h reject the large majority of
the ~127 candidates. THIS is the real gate.
2. auditCooldownMinutes — 10m suppression per mint.
3. discovery.searchQueries — how many candidates surface at all.
4. scanLimit            — this, last, and currently slack.
Widening coverage means moving 1 or 3, and both trade safety or RPC
budget for reach. Moving this number alone is close to free and close to
inert.
NOTE ON '15 tokens per 15-second pass (60/min)': intervalSeconds is 30,
not 15, and a pass measures 47-63s, so passes already overrun the timer
and ticks are skipped while busy (every tick in the sampled log carried a
skip count). At ~27s per token across 4 concurrent workers, 15 tokens is
~101s of audit work plus fixed discovery cost, so raising the ceiling
makes each pass LONGER rather than the loop faster. 60 tokens/min is not
reachable on this cadence at this RPC budget by changing this number.

_note: Turns a channel recap win into a watchlist of launch buyers, then tests
them forward.
THE STATISTICAL WARNING THAT MATTERS MOST. These wallets are selected
BECAUSE they were in a token that won — selection on the outcome, which
on its own establishes nothing. Every buyer of a 42x looks brilliant
afterwards, including the ones who bought a hundred rugs the same week
and never appear in a recap. Recap channels compound it by publishing
winners and omitting losers, so the input is a biased sample of a biased
sample.
An alpha score is therefore a REASON TO WATCH a wallet, not evidence
about it. The forward record is what converts one into the other: every
later graded buy awards forwardWinPoints or deducts forwardLossPoints,
so a wallet that got lucky once decays instead of keeping a permanent
credential. Loss points exceed win points on purpose — the measured base
rate is ~77% rugged, so symmetric scoring would drift upward on noise.
COST CONTROL: harvesting walks the pool back to genesis, which on a token
that ran 42x is tens of pages before a single transaction is fetched.
minMultiplierToHarvest keeps that walk off small recaps, genesisMaxPages
bounds it, and requireGenesis refuses to credit launch-buyer alpha when
the cap was hit — a partial walk finds buyers who are early-ish, not
early, and crediting them fills the protected list with latecomers.
MEASURED on $RAVECAT (42x): 25 pages did NOT reach genesis and the
engine correctly refused to credit; 250 pages reached it in 69 pages and
53 seconds. 25 was far too low to harvest the exact tokens this targets.
KNOWN LIMITATION — POOL GENESIS IS NOT TOKEN LAUNCH. For a pump.fun
token that graduated, the Raydium/pumpswap pool is CREATED at migration,
so walking it back finds migration-era buyers, not the bonding-curve
buyers who entered before it. Those earlier trades went through the
bonding-curve program and are invisible to a pool walk entirely.
The same RAVECAT run returned 4 genesis buyers, ALL of them without an
attributable entry price — the first transactions on a fresh pool are
liquidity operations rather than ordinary swaps, so filterLaunchWindow
excluded every one. That is the guard working, but it means the harvest
will often credit nobody on graduated tokens. Reaching true launch buyers
requires replaying the bonding-curve program, which is a different
traversal and is not implemented here.
mega_win_protected wallets survive pruneObservations even with zero
surviving buys. The whole point of tracking them is what they do NEXT,
which can be months away, so ageing them out would discard the record
exactly while waiting for the thing it exists for. Their buy history
still ages normally; only the wallet row and its score persist.
Conviction ladder mapping score to a recommended SOL size, rendered as a
bold line in every BUY alert.
ON THE NAME: this is a fixed ladder, NOT the Kelly criterion. Kelly is
f* = (bp - q)/b and needs a win probability and a payoff ratio; neither
exists at the moment of alert. The nearest measured input is the
post-mortem base rate — currently ~77% rugged across 2,500+ graded
tokens — and fed to Kelly honestly that returns a NEGATIVE fraction,
i.e. 'do not size this'. The ladder is a deliberate human override of
that arithmetic, which is a legitimate choice, but it is not a derived
optimum and should not be described as one.
WHAT THE LADDER DOES NOT KNOW: your bankroll, your open exposure, or
pool depth. 2 SOL into an 800 SOL pool is nothing; 2 SOL into a 12 SOL
pool is most of the float and moves the price against you on the way in
AND on the way out. The alert therefore prints the size as a percentage
of the pool, and warns above thinPoolWarnPct — it does NOT shrink the
size, because the number you configured is the number you get.
The top rung is reached on score alone. Cabal Swarm and Jito Block #0
decorate its label rather than gating it, so a 95 earned on clean
fundamentals is not silently sized like a 75.
_poolImpactCapNote: POOL IMPACT CAP. No recommendation may exceed maxPoolSharePct of the
pool's SOL side, whatever the score. The ladder proposes; the pool
disposes.
This REVERSES the previous behaviour, where the configured number was
always the number you got and depth was only a warning. The warning was
the wrong instrument: it is one line of text, while the cost it warns
about is quadratic in your share of the pool and is paid TWICE — walking
the price up on the way in and down on the way out, on a book with
nobody on the other side.
MEASURED against 76 live scanned tokens: median pool 20.3 SOL, so the 2.0
SOL top rung exceeds 5% on 61.8% of them and the 0.75 rung on 47.4%. This
is the binding constraint about half the time on this token population,
not an occasional edge case.
UNKNOWN DEPTH FAILS CLOSED. requireKnownPoolDepth was set true on
2026-08-09: a cap cannot be applied to a number that does not exist, so
rather than pass an uncapped size through with a disclaimer, no size is
recommended at all on those tokens. The 5% guarantee is now absolute —
there is no path by which a recommended size exceeds it.
WHAT THAT COSTS: measured, 15.6% of live scanned pairs publish no SOL-side
liquidity figure, so roughly one alert in six now carries no RECOMMENDED
BUY SIZE line. The rest of the alert is unaffected and the trade links
still render — they simply arrive without a pre-filled amount, so the size
is a decision you make rather than one the sizer makes blind. Set this
back to false to restore the previous behaviour, where such tokens got the
full ladder size with the alert stating the cap could not be applied.
minViableSol is where a capped size stops being a position and becomes a
gesture. Below it the alert recommends nothing at all rather than printing
'0.01 SOL' with a straight face.

_note: Watches for 429s and quota-exhaustion bodies from Helius, CoinGecko,
RugCheck and DexScreener, and sends one Telegram warning per provider
per cooldown window.
WHY IT EXISTS: a throttled key does not announce itself, it degrades
quietly. The whale sync derived 48/48 PnL figures on one run and 22/48
an hour later purely from request pacing, and the CoinGecko resolver
recorded WIF, JUP and BONK as not-a-Solana-token when its lookups 429d.
Both kept running and produced a worse answer that looked exactly like a
normal one. That silent loss of fidelity is what this catches.
minEventsToAlert exists because a single 429 is ordinary backpressure
that self-corrects; alerting on it would train the alert to be ignored.
An EXHAUSTED classification (a quota message in the body, or HTTP 402)
alerts on the first occurrence regardless — that one does not recover on
its own and needs a new key.
The cooldown is persisted to .state/ because every scan is a fresh
process; an in-memory guard would re-alert on every single run.

_auditConcurrencyNote: How many tokens are ANALYSED at once. Only the analysis is parallel — it is
network-bound (security fetch, buyer replay, deployer audit, funder
tracing) and that is where the ~27s per token goes.
Side effects stay SEQUENTIAL and in candidate order: notes, alerts,
positions, the digest and the console log. Parallelising those buys
nothing and breaks things that matter — interleaved log lines,
nondeterministic digest ordering, and check-then-act races across awaits
in the alert cooldown and the position opener.
RAISING THIS MULTIPLIES RPC PRESSURE by the same factor. Helius already
429s under load in this pipeline (measured in the whale sync and the
CoinGecko resolver), so 4 is deliberately modest. If audits start failing
or buyer replays come back empty, lower it before anything else.
_auditCooldownNote: Audit cooldown shield. A mint audited within this window is skipped when
selecting candidates, so each tick spends its budget on tokens it has not
WHY IT MATTERS: discovery surfaces ~130 candidates and the scan audits
6-10, sorted by 1h volume. That sort barely changes between ticks, so
without a cooldown the same handful is re-audited every ~50 seconds while
~120 others are never looked at once.
WHAT IT COSTS: a token audited at 60/100 that becomes a 90 two minutes
later is not re-scored for up to 10 minutes, so its alert is delayed by
that much. Worth it only because the never-seen pile is ~12x larger than
the seen one. Lower this if you would rather re-check known movers often;
raise it to widen coverage further.
NOT AFFECTED: explicit --token audits (CLI, channel listener, /audit bot
command) always run and never consume a cooldown slot. Open positions are
priced by sell_notifier every tick independently of the scan, so this can
